newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle docks with Russia's Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle docks with Russia's Mir.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis linked up with Russia's Mir space station on Friday to swap crew members and deliver much-needed repair gear.

The winged, reusable spaceship docked with the sprawling space station at 10:33 p.m. EDT (0233 GMT) as the two craft soared more than 180 miles (290 km) above Europe. It was the shuttle's sixth docking with Mir.
"That was a perfect-looking docking," mission control's Chris Hadfield told the shuttle crew after the docking ports of the two spacecraft slipped together, moments before orbital sunrise.
"It's great to back here on Mir, it's a beautiful sight out the window," said shuttle commander Charles Precourt, making his second visit to the space station.

Atlantis was carrying British-born astronaut Michael Foale to replace Jerry Linenger, Mir's current NASA resident. Foale, a 40-year-old astrophysicist, was to stay four months at the Russian orbital outpost.
"Welcome to your doorstep of your home," Linenger told Foale over a radio link as they waved and snapped pictures of each other through the windows of their spacecraft.
Since joining the Mir crew in January, Linenger has endured a string of serious mechanical breakdowns, one of which triggered a brief but serious fire.
Despite the problems, Foale, who holds dual British and U.S. citizenship, said he had no qualms about living on Mir.

He told Britain's BBC television on Friday that he was looking forward to "living calmly and easily in space," and that while there were similarities between life on Mir and his time at a strict English boarding school, "it could be a less stressful experience."
Foale was to relieve Linenger from duty soon after the hatches between the two spacecraft were opened at about 12:30 a.m. EDT (0430 GMT) on Saturday.
Linenger, a 42-year-old medical doctor and Navy captain, was to return to Earth aboard Atlantis on May 24. His wife, Kathryn, is expecting their second child in June.
The shuttle arrived at Mir carrying a record 4,000 pounds (1,800 kg) of supplies and equipment, including repair gear to patch up a leaky cooling system and an oxygen generator, called Elektron.
The bulky generator, about the size of an electric water heater, will be one of the first items moved across to Mir.
"It is the number-one transfer item," Jim Van Laak, deputy head of NASA's shuttle-Mir programme, said.

The Elektron was a last-minute addition to Atlantis' cargo. The Russian space authorities rushed it to the shuttle's launch site after problems with Mir's life support systems. The device uses electricity to generate breathing oxygen from waste water and will provide a crucial backup to an older, ailing system.
Foale will become the fifth NASA astronaut to live on Mir. He will be followed by two more U.S. astronauts.
